title: The Master and Margarita
author: Mikhail Bulgakov
openingChapterLabel: Part One, Chapter 1 — Never talk to strangers
openingText: At the hour of a hot spring sunset, two citizens appeared at Patriarch’s Ponds. The first of them—about forty, dressed in a grayish summer suit—was short, dark-haired, plump and bald; he carried his respectable pork-pie hat in his hand, and his neatly shaven face was adorned with glasses of supernatural size in black horn-rimmed frames. The second—a broad-shouldered, reddish, tousle-haired young man with a checked cap pushed to the back of his head—wore a cowboy shirt, crumpled white trousers and black canvas shoes.
about:
The Master and Margarita opens on a hot spring evening in Moscow, where the editor Berlioz is explaining to the young poet Ivan Bezdomny that Jesus never existed. A foreigner sits down beside them, says that he was there when Pontius Pilate questioned the prisoner Yeshua, and tells Berlioz how he will die that evening. The foreigner is Woland, a professor of black magic. With a lanky jester in a checked jacket, a fanged red-haired thug and an enormous talking cat, he spends the next few days turning literary, theatrical and bureaucratic Moscow upside down. In the clinic where Ivan ends up, Ivan meets a nameless patient, the master, who wrote a novel about Pilate and was broken by the critics. The second part belongs to Margarita, the woman who loves him, and to what she is willing to do to get him back.

The book is really two novels woven together. Between the Moscow chapters runs the master’s novel about Pilate in Yershalaim, a city Bulgakov writes in a slow, solemn, concrete prose quite unlike the comedy of the Moscow chapters. The two stories meet in the end.

Mikhail Bulgakov worked on the novel from 1928 until his death in March 1940, rewriting it many times; in 1930 he told the Soviet government in a letter that he had thrown a draft of a novel about the devil into the stove. It could not be published in his lifetime. A censored version appeared in the magazine Moskva in 1966–67, and a full text followed in the Soviet Union only in 1973. Tinct’s editions are translated directly from the Russian text prepared by Lidia Yanovskaya and published in 1990.

angleCards.title: The devil as auditor.
angleCards.text: Woland’s troupe does not tempt anyone into evil. They take Moscow at its word: hand out money and watch who grabs it, offer free Paris dresses and watch who undresses, pretend to be bribed and see who takes the bribe. The comedy is an audit of greed, cowardice and lies, carried out by the devil with remarkable fairness.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to follow Woland’s visits to the Variety, the writers’ house and the building on Sadovaya Street, and see what each of his tricks reveals about the people it is played on.

angleCards.title: Pilate’s cowardice.
angleCards.text: The procurator likes the prisoner and does not want him dead. He signs the sentence anyway, because the alternative is risking his own position. Yeshua’s last recorded words count cowardice among the worst of human vices, and the Yershalaim chapters follow Pilate as he tries to undo what cannot be undone.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read the Yershalaim chapters as the story of Pilate’s choice: what he knew, what he feared, what he did afterward, and whether the novel ever lets him go.

angleCards.title: A writer under pressure.
angleCards.text: The master writes the one book he has to write, and the literary establishment destroys him for it. Around him are the comfortable writers of Massolit, with their dachas, vouchers and restaurant. Bulgakov, who could not publish the novel in his lifetime, gives Woland the line that the book is famous for: manuscripts don’t burn.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to watch how the novel treats writing: the master’s novel, Ivan’s bad poems, the writers at Griboyedov’s, and what it means for a book to survive the person who wrote it.

angleCards.title: Margarita’s bargain.
angleCards.text: Margarita agrees to serve as hostess at Satan’s ball because it might bring the master back. Courage and love drive the second half of the novel, but so does mercy: when Margarita is finally offered whatever she wants, what she asks for is not what anyone expects.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to follow Margarita from her unhappy marriage to the ball and beyond, and see what the novel thinks love, loyalty and mercy can achieve when the devil is the one keeping score.

cast.name: Woland
cast.description: A foreign professor of black magic who arrives in Moscow in spring, with mismatched eyes, a cane topped with a poodle’s head and a retinue of three. He says he was present when Pilate questioned Yeshua and that he once breakfasted with Kant. He takes over a dead man’s apartment, gives a black magic show at the Variety Theater and seems to know everyone’s secrets. He is courteous, ironic and not cruel for its own sake.

cast.name: The master
cast.description: A former museum historian who won a lottery, gave up his job and wrote a novel about Pontius Pilate in a basement flat. When an excerpt appeared in print, the critics fell on him, and he lost his nerve, his novel and finally his freedom. He refuses to give his name, calling himself only a master, the title Margarita gave him. When Ivan meets him in the clinic he has given up hope.

cast.name: Margarita Nikolayevna
cast.description: Thirty years old, married to a kind and prominent specialist, and comfortably off, Margarita has never loved her husband. She met the master on a Moscow street, carrying yellow flowers, and became the first reader of his novel. Months after he vanished, she still does not know whether he is alive. The second part of the book is hers.

cast.name: Ivan Bezdomny
cast.description: Ivan Nikolayevich Ponyrev, a young poet who writes under the pen name Bezdomny, meaning “homeless.” He has written an anti-religious poem to order and sees Berlioz die after a conversation with a foreigner on a park bench. Nobody believes his account, and he ends up in a psychiatric clinic. There he meets the master, gives up poetry and starts to think about what he has seen.

cast.name: Pontius Pilate
cast.description: Rome’s governor of Judea, a former cavalry commander known as the Golden Spear. He hates Yershalaim and the smell of rose oil, suffers from crippling headaches and is attached to no one but his dog, Banga. On the morning of the fourteenth of Nisan he questions a prisoner he finds he cannot dismiss, and spends the rest of the novel living with what he decides.

cast.name: Yeshua Ha-Notsri
cast.description: A wandering philosopher from Gamala, brought before Pilate beaten and bound on the charge of inciting the people to destroy the temple. He insists that there are no evil people in the world, and says that every kind of power is a form of violence against people. His only follower, Levi Matvei, writes down his words and gets them wrong.

whyItMatters.title: Comedy as a way of telling the truth
whyItMatters.body: Much of the novel is extremely funny: a master of ceremonies whose head is torn off and put back on, a cat who pays his tram fare, an empty suit that goes on signing documents, an office whose staff cannot stop singing. The comedy is aimed at a real city, Moscow around 1930, with its shared apartments, its housing committees, its informers, its literary bureaucracy and its sudden arrests that nobody explains. Bulgakov could not say any of this directly. He has the devil do it, and the narrator report it with a straight face. The result is one of the rare books that is satirical and lyrical at once, and the laughter does not take the edge off what it exposes. Woland’s verdict on the Muscovites after the show at the Variety is that they are people like any other people: they love money, they are frivolous, mercy sometimes knocks at their hearts, and the housing problem has spoiled them.

whyItMatters.title: What cowardice costs
whyItMatters.body: At the center of the master’s novel is a man who knows what is right and does not do it. Pilate is not a monster. He likes Yeshua, he looks for a way out, he tries to bargain, and when the bargain fails he signs. Afterward he does everything in his power to make amends, and none of it changes what he did. Bulgakov wrote this story while working under censorship, with friends being arrested and colleagues denouncing one another, and every Moscow chapter repeats the question on a smaller scale: the critic who attacks a book he knows is good, the neighbor who informs for the sake of an apartment, the official who says what he is expected to say. The novel is hard on cowardice and unusually patient with the cowards themselves.

whyItMatters.title: Two worlds that answer each other
whyItMatters.body: The Moscow chapters are noisy, crowded and fast; the Yershalaim chapters are slow, hot and almost silent. Bulgakov wrote them as if they belonged to different books, and the reader feels the shift every time. Yet the two stories keep echoing each other: a full moon over both cities, a storm that breaks over both, a man who betrays a friend for his own gain in each, a writer and a prisoner who both pay for telling the truth. Reading one illuminates the other. By the final chapters the two stories, and the people in them, meet, and the novel’s last pages belong to both.
